57.title: Palms (Matthew 21:1–11)
57.hook: he rides in on a donkey and the crowd throws coats on the road
57.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday Catholics receive blessed palms, walk in procession, and hear the Passion read; many keep the palms at home until they are burned for the next Ash Wednesday, and every Mass sings hosanna in the Sanctus.

segments.voice: Last week ended at Lazarus's tomb, and the line Jesus wept. Did you let yourself grieve? Day fifty-seven. Now the road reaches Jerusalem. This is Holy Week.

Picture a parade. Presidents arrive in armored cars. Conquering generals in Rome rode in chariots, and kings entered cities on war horses. Everybody could see the power. Now it's springtime, just before Passover, and Jerusalem is packed with pilgrims. Jesus sends two disciples to a village on the Mount of Olives to fetch something for his entrance. Not a horse. A donkey, and her colt. They throw their cloaks over them and he sits on them. And the crowd goes wild. They spread their coats on the road in front of him. They cut branches from the trees and lay them down. And they shout one word, over and over. Today's word is what they shouted.
screen: `KINGS RIDE WAR HORSES.` → `HE SENDS FOR A DONKEY.` → `COATS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's what the crowds cried, going before him and following, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, from a line in Psalm one hundred eighteen: hoshia na. Save, please. Save us now. It began as a cry for help, and over time it became a shout of praise, like a cheer. Both meanings are in the air that day: help us, and hooray. And the donkey is not an accident. Matthew says it happened to fulfill the prophet Zechariah: "Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass." A king, but a meek one. A king who comes in peace, not on a war horse. The whole city is stirred up, Matthew says, asking: who is this? And the crowds answer: this is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee. The Church relives this day every year on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week. Palms are blessed, and people carry them in procession into the church. Then, in the same Mass, the whole Passion is read, and the mood turns. The crowd's hosanna and the cross are held together on one day. Many Catholics take their blessed palms home, tuck them behind a crucifix, and bring them back the next year, when old palms are burned to make the ashes for Ash Wednesday. And every Mass, all year, Catholics sing this crowd's words in the Holy, Holy, Holy: hosanna in the highest.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wave one small welcome today. Settle and breathe. Think about who is arriving in your day. A child coming home from school. A coworker walking in late. A neighbor, a guest, a stranger at the door. Most arrivals get a glance, or nothing. Choose one person, and picture giving them a real welcome: eyes up, a smile, their name. Not a parade. Just a coat on the road. If you pray, you can say the crowd's word, hosanna, as praise or as a cry for help. The bell holds the time.
Hosanna. From Hebrew: save us, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: a king on a donkey. Today, notice where power could show off, and choose the gentle way instead. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: The tables overturned (Matthew 21:12–13)
58.hook: the one time he makes a whip, and it's about the house of prayer
58.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of the cleansing of the Temple on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year B, and many treat the season as a time to clear out habits and clutter to make room for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: the crowd's cry as a king rode in on a donkey. Your line was a king on a donkey. Did you choose the gentle way? Day fifty-eight. Today the gentle king does something that shocks everyone.

Picture the outer courts of the Temple in Jerusalem during the festival. Enormous, noisy, and packed. Pilgrims have come from all over the world. They need animals for the sacrifices, so there are people selling cattle and sheep and doves. They need the right coins to pay the Temple tax, so there are money changers at their tables, swapping foreign money. The shouting, the bargaining, the animals, the clink of coins. And Jesus walks in. The man who has spent weeks of our story healing, forgiving, eating with sinners, telling stories of lost sheep. And he starts turning over tables. Today: the day the gentle teacher got angry.
screen: `THE TEMPLE COURTS AT FESTIVAL.` → `SELLERS AND MONEY CHANGERS.` → `HE TURNS OVER THE TABLES.`

segments.voice: Matthew says Jesus went into the Temple and cast out all who were buying and selling there, and overthrew the tables of the money changers, and the seats of those who sold doves. Coins rolling across the stone floor. Birds fluttering. People shouting. And then he quotes scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves." He's joining two prophets. Isaiah, who promised that God's house would be a house of prayer, and Mark adds, for all nations. And Jeremiah, who warned against treating the Temple like a hideout for robbers. So this isn't Jesus against the Temple. It's a Jewish teacher who loves the Temple, standing in the line of Israel's own prophets, demanding that it be what it's for. The whip is in John's Gospel: John says he made a whip of cords and drove out the animals. It's the only time in the Gospels he picks up anything like a weapon, and it's to clear a space for prayer. And watch what happens next in Matthew, right after the tables go over. The blind and the lame come to him in the Temple, and he heals them. The space gets cleared, and then it gets filled, with the people who needed it most. Catholics hear another layer too. Saint Paul writes that you yourselves are God's temple, and that his Spirit lives in you. The Church reads John's version of this story in Lent, a season for clearing out the clutter so there's room for prayer.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one cluttered space. Settle and breathe. Think of a space in your life that's meant for one thing and has filled up with everything else. A desk. A corner of your room. The first ten minutes of your morning, eaten by the phone. Your own head. Pick one. Picture the tables going over, gently: the clutter cleared, and the space open again. What would you want that space to be for? If you pray, you can ask for a house of prayer inside you. The bell holds the time.
The tables overturned. Jesus clearing the Temple courts, so the house of prayer could be a house of prayer again. Today's word.
Your line: a house of prayer. Today, clear one cluttered space, a drawer or a morning, and leave it open for something better. Day fifty-eight.

59.title: The perfume (Mark 14:3–9)
59.hook: a woman breaks a jar worth a year's wages over his head and he defends her
59.carry: she has done a beautiful thing
59.howItsDone: Catholics hear the anointing at Bethany in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Mark, and the Church's anointings with holy oils, at baptism, confirmation and ordination, echo the meaning of the word Christ, the anointed one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tables overturned in the Temple courts. Your line was a house of prayer. What space did you clear? Day fifty-nine. Two days before the Passover, in Bethany.

A dinner in Bethany, at the house of a man called Simon the leper. Jesus is reclining at the table with friends. Everyone knows the religious authorities are looking for a way to arrest him. The air is heavy. And a woman walks in holding a small alabaster jar. Inside is pure nard, a perfume made from a plant that grows far away in the Himalayas. It's worth, someone says, more than three hundred denarii. Nearly a year's wages. And she doesn't open it. She breaks it. Snaps the neck of the jar, and pours the whole thing over his head. The smell fills the room. Nobody can pretend it didn't happen. Today: the perfume.
screen: `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `AN ALABASTER JAR OF NARD.` → `SHE BREAKS IT OVER HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Some of the guests are furious. Why this waste? That could have been sold, and the money given to the poor. And they scold her. It sounds like a good point. It's the kind of thing we'd say. But Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." The Greek is kalon ergon, and kalon means both good and beautiful. That's why many modern translations say, she has done a beautiful thing. He says: you'll always have the poor with you, and you can help them whenever you want. That's not dismissing the poor; he's echoing the Law of Moses, which says there will always be poor people, so open your hand to them. But me, he says, you won't always have. She has done what she could. She's anointed my body ahead of time, for burial. She understood what was coming when the others didn't. And then one of the most astonishing promises in the Gospels: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memorial of her." And here we are, telling it. Yet Mark never gives her name. John tells a similar story and says it was Mary of Bethany, Martha's sister. For centuries in the West, after a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was also thought to be Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar now treats them as separate women. One more thing: anointing someone's head was what you did for a king. Messiah means anointed one. She's the one who does it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something lavishly. Settle and breathe. We're good at giving the sensible amount. The polite gift, the right-sized favor. Think of one person who deserves more than sensible. Someone who's carrying something heavy right now. What could you give them that's a little extravagant? Your whole evening. A long letter. Real attention, with the phone in another room. Picture breaking the jar. If you pray, you can offer God something lavish too: time, or thanks. The bell holds the time.
The perfume. A jar broken over his head, a room full of scent, and a woman remembered wherever the story is told. Today's word.
Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. Today, give one gift that's a little more than sensible. Day fifty-nine.

60.title: The basin and towel (John 13:1–15)
60.hook: at the last supper he kneels and washes their feet
60.carry: as I have done to you
60.howItsDone: At the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest washes the feet of members of the congregation, a rite called the Mandatum, after the Gospel of John 13 is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the perfume, a jar broken over his head. Your line was she has done a beautiful thing. What did you give lavishly? Day sixty. Today, the last supper, and a towel.

Think about feet in that world. Sandals, dusty roads, animals on the streets. When guests arrived for a meal, someone washed their feet. It was one of the lowest jobs in the house, usually left to a servant, or guests washed their own. A host did not kneel to do it. Now it's the night before Jesus dies. He's at supper with his closest friends, and he knows it's the last. John begins the scene with a sentence like a doorway, in the Douay-Rheims: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Unto the end. To the very last. And then, in the middle of the meal, he gets up from the table. Today: the basin and the towel.
screen: `DUSTY FEET, THE LOWEST JOB.` → `THE LAST SUPPER.` → `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: John slows down and gives every movement. He rises from supper. He lays aside his outer garments. He takes a towel and ties it around his waist. He pours water into a basin. And he begins to wash the disciples' feet, and to dry them with the towel. The teacher is on his knees, doing the servant's job, going from one friend to the next. And John has already told us that Judas, who will betray him, is at that table. His feet get washed too. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it. Lord, are you going to wash my feet? Jesus says: you don't understand now, but you will. And Peter: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." And Peter, all or nothing as always: then not only my feet, Lord, but my hands and my head. When he's finished, Jesus puts his garments back on, sits down, and asks: do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you're right. So if I've washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's. "For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you do also." Catholics relive this on Holy Thursday, at the Mass of the Lord's Supper. In many parishes, the priest takes off his outer vestment, kneels, and washes the feet of people from the parish. The rite's old Latin name is the Mandatum, from Jesus's new commandment later that night, and that word is where the English name Maundy Thursday comes from.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one humble task for someone. Settle and breathe. Think of the jobs nobody wants in your home, your office, your group. Cleaning the bathroom. Taking out the recycling. Staying late to put the chairs away. Changing the diaper. Pick one you could do today for someone else, without being asked, and without mentioning it afterward. Picture yourself doing it slowly, with care, the way John describes the towel and the basin. If you pray, you can offer it for that person. The bell holds the time.
The basin and towel. The night before he died, Jesus knelt and washed his friends' feet, and told them to do the same. Today's word.
Your line: as I have done to you. Today, do the humble task quietly, and let nobody thank you for it. Day sixty.

61.title: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46)
61.hook: he asks the cup to pass, then not my will but thine; they fall asleep
61.howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night many Catholic parishes keep the Blessed Sacrament at an altar of repose so people can watch and pray with Jesus, and many Catholics keep a regular holy hour before the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the basin and towel: at the last supper he knelt and washed their feet. Your line was as I have done to you. What small, humble thing did you do for someone? Day sixty-one.

Supper is over. They sing a hymn, and they walk out of the city in the dark, down across a little valley and up into an olive grove on the far side. Eleven of them now. Jesus leaves most of them near the entrance and takes three further in: Peter, James and John. And then he says something none of them has ever heard him say. In the Douay-Rheims: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." The one who calmed storms is asking his friends not to leave him alone. Then he goes a few steps further, falls on his face, and prays. Today's word is the name of that garden.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, IN THE DARK.` → `PETER, JAMES AND JOHN.` → `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Gethsemane most likely comes from Aramaic words for an oil press. It was a place where olives were crushed until the oil ran out. Christians have noticed that for a long time. Now the prayer: "My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me. Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The chalice, the cup, is an old biblical picture for what life pours out for you to drink, and here it means the suffering coming at dawn. Notice he asks. He doesn't pretend he wants it. Luke even says his sweat fell like drops of blood. The Church teaches that Jesus had a real human will, and this is where you can hear it: a man who does not want to die, handing himself over anyway. Luke puts it in the words of today's line: not my will, but thine be done. Then he walks back, and the three are asleep. "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" He isn't furious. He almost makes excuses for them: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Three times he prays. Three times they sleep. That one hour has stayed with Catholics. On the night of Holy Thursday, after the evening Mass, many churches keep the Blessed Sacrament at a side altar and people come to watch with him, late into the night. And the old practice of a holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist, grows from that same question.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay awake with someone's pain. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is carrying something heavy right now: an illness, a loss, a fear. You can't fix it. That's not the job tonight. The job is only to stay. Hold them in your mind and don't drift off to your own list. When you notice you've wandered, come back, the way he came back to his sleeping friends. If you pray, you can simply pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane. The olive grove across the valley, whose name probably means oil press, where he prayed and his friends slept. Today's word.
Your line: not my will. Today, when something doesn't go your way, say the whole thing honestly first, the way he did, and then see if you can let it go. Day sixty-one.

62.title: Peter's three denials (Luke 22:54–62)
62.hook: a servant girl asks, a cock crows, and the Lord turns and looks at Peter
62.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Peter's denial in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and many bring their own failures to God in the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane, the oil press: let this chalice pass, and his friends asleep. Your line was not my will. Did you get to say the honest thing first, and then let go? Day sixty-two.

It's the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Peter, the one who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, has followed at a distance, all the way into the courtyard. Somebody has lit a fire. It's cold. Peter sits down with the others around it, trying to look like everyone else. And a servant girl, one of the house staff, looks at him in the firelight. Looks again. And says, to the whole circle, this man was with him too. Peter answers before he thinks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, I know him not." That's the first one. Today: the whole night, and the look at the end of it.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE COURTYARD.` → `A SERVANT GIRL LOOKS TWICE.` → `WOMAN, I KNOW HIM NOT.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in three quick blows. The girl. Then a little later, another person: you're one of them. Peter: I am not. Then about an hour passes, and a third insists: this man was with him, for he's a Galilean too. And Peter says he doesn't even know what the man is talking about. While he's still speaking, a rooster crows. Now the verse only Luke has: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." Jesus is somewhere in that courtyard, under guard, close enough to turn. And Peter remembers what Jesus told him at supper, that before the cock crowed he would deny him three times. "And Peter going out, wept bitterly." Here's the honest part: Luke never tells us what that look was like. The text is silent. But Christians have read it for centuries as a look of mercy, not anger, because of what comes after. Peter isn't written off. He weeps, and he doesn't vanish: on Easter morning, Luke says, he's the one who runs to the tomb. And this is the part Catholics hold on to: this is the same Peter Jesus called the rock. The first pope, in Catholic teaching, is a man who failed his friend three times in one night and was not given up on. The Church was built on someone who knew exactly how much he needed mercy. That's why Catholics say a failure is never the last word, and why they say confession exists: you go out, you weep, and you come back.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a time you let a friend down. Settle and breathe. Let one moment come back, not the worst one, just a real one: a time you went quiet when you should have spoken, or said you didn't know someone you did. Don't argue with it. Just let it be true. Then picture a look coming toward you across the courtyard. Not anger. Something that knows, and stays. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in your own plain words. The bell holds the time.
Peter's three denials. A servant girl, a stranger, an accent, a rooster, and one look across a courtyard. Today's word.
Your line: the look was not anger. Today, when you catch yourself failing at something small, see if you can look at yourself the way Christians say he looked at Peter. Day sixty-two.

63.title: Before Pilate (John 18:28–19:16)
63.hook: Pilate asks what is truth and washes his hands
63.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of the trial before Pilate every Good Friday, and they name Pilate each Sunday when they profess the Creed at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's three denials, the rooster, and the Lord turning to look. Your line was the look was not anger. Could you look at your own small failure that way? Day sixty-three.

Early morning. Jesus is led to the headquarters of the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Rome holds the power of death here, not anyone else. And what follows is almost a stage play. Pilate walks outside to the crowd, then back inside to his prisoner, then out again, then in again. Seven times, if you count, the scene shifts. Outside, voices getting louder. Inside, a quiet man in chains, and a governor who can't work out who he is. And here's a strange thing: every Sunday, Catholics say this man's name. In the Creed, a few words after the name of Mary, there he is. The old Apostles' Creed puts it: suffered under Pontius Pilate. Today: the conversation inside.
screen: `THE ROMAN GOVERNOR'S HOUSE.` → `OUT TO THE CROWD, BACK TO THE PRISONER.` → `SUFFERED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.`

segments.voice: Pilate starts with the only question that matters to Rome: are you a king? A king is a rival. Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." Pilate presses. And Jesus says he was born and came into the world to give testimony to the truth, and that everyone who is of the truth hears his voice. Then Pilate says the line: "What is truth?" And he doesn't wait. John says he goes straight back out. Maybe it's a sneer. Maybe it's tired. Maybe it's the most honest question in the story. The text doesn't tell us his tone. There's a later wordplay people love: in Latin the question is quid est veritas, and if you shuffle those letters you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. Nobody in the story says that. But it's the Christian answer: the truth was standing in front of him. Pilate says three times he finds no fault in him. And still he hands him over to be crucified. Matthew adds the picture everyone remembers: Pilate takes water and washes his hands in front of the crowd, as if that settled it. It didn't. The Church has always said Rome carried out the execution, and teaches plainly that the Jewish people as a whole, then or now, can never be blamed for it. The hands were washed. The choice was still his.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.` · `WHAT IS TRUTH? HE DOESN'T WAIT.` · `NO FAULT IN HIM, AND HANDED OVER.` · `WATER DOESN'T WASH A CHOICE.` · then, large: `WHAT IS TRUTH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you wash your hands of things. Settle and breathe. Think about the last few weeks. Was there a moment you knew something wasn't right and said, not my problem? A group chat that turned cruel. A coworker being talked about. A thing you could have said and didn't. No need to punish yourself. Just see it clearly, the way you'd see water running over your hands. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to answer the question Pilate walked away from. The bell holds the time.
Before Pilate. The Roman governor who asked what truth is, found no fault, and washed his hands anyway. Today's word.

Your line: what is truth. That's Holy Week: palms, the tables, the perfume, the basin, the garden, the denials, and Pilate. Today, when you're tempted to walk away from a hard question, stay one more minute. Day sixty-three.

fork.setup: you're Pilate. you find no fault in this man, and the crowd outside is getting louder. what do you do?
options: set him free and face the crowd.
wash your hands and hand him over.
send him away to someone else's court.
fork.reveal: he washes his hands in front of the crowd and hands Jesus over to be crucified. the water didn't make it someone else's choice.

original.note: Greek: truth. often explained as un-hiddenness, what is out in the open.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate washed his hands, so it wasn't his fault.
what it means: a man in power finds no fault, walks away from the question of truth, and hands him over anyway.
what a scholar hears: quid est veritas, and the later anagram est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. and Rome, not a people, carried out the execution.
